items: 1Describe the Fluid Mosaic Model of the plasma membrane, including the amphipathic phospholipid bilayer, cholesterol, glycolipids and the proteins embedded in it.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Plasma membrane The boundary membrane surrounding a cell, separating it from its external environment. It consists of a phospholipid bilayer plus associated membrane lipids and proteins. Every organelle is also surrounded by its own biomembrane with a unique protein complement, enabling organelle-specific functions.
Cytoplasm vs. cytosol Cytoplasm is everything inside the plasma membrane but outside the nucleus. Cytosol is the aqueous portion of the cytoplasm that lies outside all the membrane-bound organelles.

Cell fractionation
A technique for investigating organelle function by disrupting cells and separating them into their components — homogenisation, fractionation (separation), then analysis.

Rf value (chromatography) Rf = distance travelled by a component ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front, both measured from the origin. It is characteristic and reproducible for a compound under identical conditions, so it is used to identify substances.
Fluid Mosaic Model & Lipids→ Membrane Proteins & Permeability→ Homogenisation→ Centrifugation→ Spectrophotometry / Autoradiography / Chromatography
Membrane architecture
The plasma membrane is described as a fluid structure with a "mosaic" of proteins embedded within it — phospholipids, cholesterol and glycolipids form the fluid matrix in which those proteins float.

Fluid Mosaic Model The membrane is a fluid structure containing a mosaic of various proteins embedded within it. Phospholipids are the most abundant membrane lipid, and they are amphipathic — each molecule has both a hydrophobic region and a hydrophilic region.
The membrane "collage"

Cholesterol, glycolipids, transmembrane proteins, cytoskeleton filaments, peripheral proteins, glycoproteins and phospholipids all sit together in the fluid lipid-bilayer matrix, forming what is often described as a "collage" of components rather than a rigid, fixed structure.

items: 1Phospholipids — the amphipathic bilayer backbone, roughly 75% of membrane lipids.
2Cholesterol — wedges between phospholipid tails, regulating fluidity.
3Glycolipids — lipids with a carbohydrate head, roughly 5% of membrane lipids, found only facing the extracellular fluid.
4Transmembrane / integral proteins — span or embed within the bilayer.
5Peripheral proteins — attached loosely to a membrane surface.
6Cytoskeleton filaments — anchor to the membrane's inner face for support and shape.

blocks.x: The phospholipid bilayer

Amphipathic orientation The polar, hydrophilic heads of phospholipids face outward, toward the water on both sides of the membrane. The nonpolar, hydrophobic fatty-acid tails face inward, away from water, packing against each other in the membrane interior.

Phosphoglycerides The principal class of phospholipid. Fatty acyl chains are esterified to two of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups; the third hydroxyl group is esterified to a phosphate group, which carries the polar head.
Membrane fluidity

items: ↔Lateral movement — phospholipids move sideways within their own leaflet very frequently, roughly 10⁷ times per second.
↕Flip-flop movement — a phospholipid crossing from one leaflet to the other is rare, occurring only about once per month for a given molecule.

blocks.x: Fatty acid saturation and fluidity Unsaturated hydrocarbon tails contain kinks (from double bonds) that prevent tight packing, increasing fluidity. Saturated tails pack tightly together, increasing viscosity and rigidity.
Temperature effects on fluidity

As temperature falls, a membrane shifts from a fluid to a more solid (gel-like) state. The exact temperature at which this solidification happens depends on the membrane's lipid composition: membranes rich in unsaturated fatty acids stay fluid at lower temperatures than membranes rich in saturated fatty acids. For proper function, a membrane needs to remain roughly as fluid as salad oil — too rigid and transport/signalling proteins cannot move or change shape; too fluid and the membrane loses structural integrity.

Cholesterol's dual role At warm temperatures (~37°C), cholesterol restrains excess phospholipid movement, reducing fluidity. At cool temperatures, cholesterol maintains fluidity by wedging between phospholipids and preventing them from packing too tightly together. Cholesterol therefore acts as a fluidity buffer across a range of temperatures.
Membrane lipid composition

c: Amphipathic; polar heads hydrophilic and face the aqueous environment on both surfaces, nonpolar tails hydrophobic and line the interior
Carbohydrate polar head; found only on the extracellular-facing side of the membrane

blocks.title: Why does membrane fluidity matter biologically?

items: Transport and receptor proteins often need to change shape or diffuse laterally to function — a membrane that is too rigid would block this.
Vesicle fusion and budding (e.g. during secretion or endocytosis) require the bilayer to bend and reseal, which needs fluidity.
Organisms living in cold environments often have membranes with a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids to stay functional at low temperature.

blocks.x: Proteins in the mosaic
Proteins give the membrane its functional identity — as channels, transporters and receptors — while the bilayer itself decides what can and cannot cross without help.
Types of membrane proteins
Integral proteins

Extend into or completely across the membrane. A protein that fully spans the bilayer is called a transmembrane protein. These proteins are themselves amphipathic — their hydrophobic portions sit embedded among the phospholipid tails, while hydrophilic portions face the aqueous environment on either side.
Peripheral proteins
Attached to the inner or outer surface of the membrane, not embedded within it. They are easily removed (e.g. by changing salt concentration or pH) without disrupting the bilayer itself.

Glycoproteins & the glycocalyx Membrane proteins with an attached sugar (carbohydrate) chain, always facing the extracellular fluid. Together with glycolipids they form the glycocalyx — a carbohydrate coat that gives a cell its molecular "uniqueness"/identity, provides stickiness for cell-cell adhesion, and traps a slippery layer of fluid at the cell surface.
What membrane proteins do

items: 1Channel formation — some integral proteins form passageways that let specific substances cross the membrane.
2Transporter proteins — bind a substance, change shape, and move it from one side of the membrane to the other.
3Receptor proteins — act as cellular recognition sites, binding specific substances (hormones, signalling molecules) to trigger a response.

blocks.x: Selective permeability

c: Small non-polar / uncharged molecules (O₂, CO₂, steroids)
Diffuse directly across the lipid bilayer
Passes through transient gaps that open as phospholipids move
Cannot cross directly — require vesicular transport (endocytosis/exocytosis)

blocks.x: Gradients across the plasma membrane

Concentration gradient A difference in the concentration of a substance across the membrane — for example, there is more O₂ and Na⁺ outside the cell, and more CO₂ and K⁺ inside the cell. Substances tend to move down their concentration gradient (high → low).
Electrical gradient (membrane potential) A difference in the distribution of charged ions inside versus outside the cell. Charged particles tend to move toward the oppositely charged region.

Electrochemical gradient For ions, the concentration gradient and the electrical gradient combine into a single electrochemical gradient, which together determines the net direction an ion tends to move.

blocks.title: Quick check — matching protein type to function

items: A protein that binds glucose, changes shape, and delivers it into the cytosol is acting as a transporter protein.
A protein that forms a continuous water-filled pore for ions to diffuse through is a channel.
A protein on the surface that binds a hormone and triggers an internal signal is a receptor protein.
A protein that can be washed off the membrane surface with a mild salt solution is most likely peripheral, not integral.

blocks.x: Step 1 of cell fractionation
Before organelles can be separated and studied, cells must first be broken open — gently enough to keep organelles intact, but thoroughly enough to release them.

Cell fractionation A technique that investigates organelle function by disrupting cells and separating them into their components, in three steps: (1) disruption/homogenisation in an iso-osmotic medium to give a homogenate, (2) fractionation — separation of cell fragments and organelles, and (3) analysis of the chemical activity of the separated fragments.
1. Homogenise (disrupt cells)→ 2. Fractionate (separate)→ 3. Analyse (chemical activity)
Cell homogenisation (lysis) methods

items: 1Mechanical disruption — rotating blades shear cells apart; a Waring blender is used for tissue, and a Polytron can handle volumes as small as 1 ml.

2Liquid homogenisation — the most widely used approach for small volumes/cultured cells; it shears membranes by forcing the cell suspension through a narrow space. Includes the Dounce homogenizer (manual glass pestle in a glass tube) and the Potter-Elvehjem homogenizer (manual or mechanical Teflon pestle in a conical vessel).

3French press — a piston applies high pressure to 40-250 ml samples, forcing them through a tiny hole; only 2 passes are needed. Expensive, but the preferred method for breaking tough bacterial cells.

4Sonication — pulsed high-frequency sound from a vibrating probe creates microscopic vapour bubbles that implode, generating shock waves that lyse cells. Applied in short bursts in an ice bath to prevent overheating; best for volumes under 100 ml.

5Freeze and thaw — sample is frozen (e.g. dry ice/ethanol bath) then thawed at room temperature or 37°C; ice crystals swell and break the cells. Requires multiple cycles; effective for releasing recombinant proteins from bacteria.

6Mortar and pestle — the most common method for plant cells: tissue is frozen in liquid nitrogen then crushed. It is the fastest way to access plant proteins/DNA given the strength of the cellulose cell wall.

c: Bulk tissue; volumes down to 1 ml
Small volumes, cultured cells (most widely used)
Pestle forces suspension through a narrow gap, shearing membranes
Piston forces sample under high pressure through a tiny hole (2 passes)
High-frequency sound creates imploding vapour bubbles, generating lysing shock waves
Ice crystal formation swells and ruptures cells over repeated cycles
Tissue frozen in liquid nitrogen, then crushed

blocks.x: Homogenisation additives

items: aHypotonic buffers — promote cell swelling and bursting.
bEnzyme digestion (~200 µg/ml) — digests the polysaccharide cell walls of yeast and bacteria before/during lysis.
cGlass beads — facilitate crushing, commonly used with yeast.
dDNase (25-50 µg/ml) / RNase (50 µg/ml) — reduce the viscosity caused by nucleic acids released from broken cells; not needed after sonication (which shears DNA itself).
eProtease inhibitors — prevent proteolysis (unwanted protein degradation) of the released contents.

blocks.title: Choosing a homogenisation method — worked scenarios

items: Breaking open bacterial cells for protein purification, expensive equipment available: French press — needs only 2 passes and is the preferred method for tough bacterial cell walls.
Releasing a recombinant protein from E. coli without specialised equipment: Freeze-thaw cycles — repeated freezing and thawing ruptures cells via ice crystal formation.
Extracting DNA from frozen plant leaf tissue: Mortar and pestle after freezing in liquid nitrogen — the fastest way past a cellulose wall.
Lysing a 50 ml culture of mammalian cells without heat damage: Sonication in short bursts in an ice bath.

blocks.x: Step 2 of cell fractionation
Once cells are broken open, their contents are separated by spinning — sedimentation rate depends on particle size, density and shape.

Two common centrifugation techniques Differential centrifugation and buoyant (density gradient) centrifugation. Both rely on the fact that sedimentation rate depends on a particle's size, density and shape.
Differential centrifugation

The homogenate undergoes repeated centrifugations at increasing centrifugal force. Each spin separates the mixture into a pellet (large, dense structures at the bottom of the tube) and a supernatant (smaller components still suspended in the liquid above). The supernatant is decanted and re-centrifuged at a progressively higher speed to collect increasingly smaller components. Separation is based primarily on particle size.
Example protocol: a cell homogenate is centrifuged step-wise. What pellets at 1000×g for 10 minutes, and what pellets after the supernatant is then spun at 10,000×g for 20 minutes?

items: 1At low speed (1000×g, 10 min), only the largest, densest structures reach the bottom.Pellet: unbroken cells and heavy nuclei
2The supernatant (still containing smaller organelles) is decanted and spun again at a higher speed.10,000×g, 20 min
3Intermediate-velocity organelles now pellet.Pellet: mitochondria, lysosomes, microbodies

blocks.x: Repeated washing, re-suspension and re-pelleting in isotonic solvents removes smaller contaminants — a preliminary step before finer density-gradient separation.
Density gradient (buoyant density) centrifugation

The preferred method for purifying subcellular organelles or macromolecules. Gradients are built from layered media (commonly sucrose), with the heaviest layer at the bottom and the lightest at the top — either discontinuous (distinct steps) or continuous gradients. For example, viruses (density 1.1-1.2 g/cm³) can be separated on a sucrose gradient: the densest components move fastest and stop where the surrounding density matches their own, banding with the least-dense components toward the top and denser ones lower down.
Rate-zonal (size) separation

Exploits differences in particle size/mass rather than density. Used, for example, to separate endosomes or antibody classes that have similar density but different mass. Centrifugation is stopped before particles reach equilibrium.
Isopycnic (equilibrium/density) separation

A particle sinks through the gradient until it reaches a position where the solution density equals its own particle density; further centrifugation has no further effect. Classic example: separating nucleic acids in a caesium chloride (CsCl) gradient.

c: Bulk separation of organelle classes (nuclei → mitochondria/lysosomes → microsomes)
Separating particles of similar density but different size, e.g. endosome subtypes, antibody classes
Separating nucleic acids in a CsCl gradient; purifying organelles/macromolecules by density

blocks.x: The analytical ultracentrifuge

Analytical ultracentrifuge A classical method that relies purely on mass and gravitational laws, requiring no comparison standards. It analyses the solution behaviour of molecules across different concentrations and solvents, and can separate/characterise very small molecules as well as macromolecules such as ribosomes and proteins. The specimen is mixed with a sucrose or CsCl medium in a quartz cell and spun at forces up to 500,000×g, sedimenting particles and forming a sharp boundary between the pure solvent and the specimen-containing solvent.

items: Differential centrifugation is a coarse, fast, step-wise separation by size, usually done first.
Density-gradient centrifugation is a finer purification step, usually done after a differential spin, to resolve organelles of similar size but different density (or vice versa).
Isopycnic separation stops naturally once a particle reaches its own density in the gradient — extra spin time does not move it further.
Rate-zonal separation depends on time — it must be stopped before particles reach equilibrium, or the size-based separation is lost.

blocks.x: Step 3 of cell fractionation
Once fractions are separated, these techniques analyse what is in them — by light absorption, by radioactive labelling, or by differential migration through a stationary phase.
Spectrophotometry

Spectrophotometer A spectrometer (produces light of a selected wavelength) combined with a photometer (measures light intensity), with a cuvette holding the liquid sample between the two. The photometer sends a voltage signal to a display (such as a galvanometer) that changes with the amount of light absorbed by the sample.

The concentration of a coloured substance is determined from the extent of light absorption at an appropriate wavelength. For example, haemoglobin appears red because it absorbs blue/green light more strongly than red light; its absorbance is proportional to haemoglobin concentration. Water-quality photometers/colorimeters are ion-specific, computer-interfaced probes that measure concentration from the intensity of a developed colour.
Autoradiography

Autoradiography A bio-analytical technique that visualises the distribution of radioactively labelled substances within tissue, cells, organelles or biomolecules. It is highly sensitive, and allows quantitative estimation via densitometry.
How an autoradiogram is made

items: 1The sample is covered with a photographic emulsion.
2Radioactive emissions from the labelled substance activate nearby silver halide crystals in the emulsion.
3Ag⁺ ions are reduced to metallic Ag atoms, forming dark bands wherever radioactivity was present.
4The slide is washed with fixers, leaving only the insoluble Ag atoms behind.
5The finished autoradiogram is examined under a microscope.

blocks.x: Mechanistically, beta particles emitted from the labelled sample penetrate the silver halide film emulsion, activating the silver, which is then reduced to detectable black silver particles. Sensitivity can be improved by detecting at 70°C and by pre-flashing the film.
Uses of autoradiography

items: 1Tissues incubated with radioactive isotopes so the label incorporates into cells; sections are then placed under photographic emulsion to record where the label ended up.
2Commonly used isotopes: tritium (³H), ¹⁴C, ³²P, ⁴⁵Ca, ³⁵S.
3Locating protein synthesis sites — using radioactive amino acid precursors that get incorporated into newly made proteins.
4Medical use — a barium meal (a barium radioisotope) is used to detect ulcers of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT).

blocks.x: Chromatography
Chromatography A technique that separates the components of a mixture based on their partitioning between a stationary phase and a moving (mobile) phase.
Partition chromatography
The stationary phase is a liquid. Separation depends on the relative solubility of components between two or more immiscible solvents (the partition coefficient).
Adsorption chromatography
The stationary phase is a solid. Separation relies mainly on electrostatic interactions between components and the solid surface.
Paper chromatography

Used to separate and identify coloured mixtures, especially pigments. Largely superseded by thin-layer chromatography (TLC), but still useful for teaching the principle. A concentrated sample is spotted about 2 cm from the base of a strip of paper (using a capillary tube); the paper is then dipped in a solvent (e.g. ethanol, water or acetone), kept below the level of the spot, inside a sealed container. The solvent rises up the paper by capillary action, carrying the sample with it. Different compounds travel at different rates because of differing solubility in the solvent and differing attraction to the cellulose fibres of the paper. This typically takes minutes to hours. Two-way chromatography — rotating the chromatogram 90° into a second solvent — is used when two or more substances share the same value in the first solvent.

Rf value ("ratio of fronts") Rf = distance travelled by a component (from the origin) ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front (from the origin). The Rf value is characteristic and reproducible for a given compound under identical conditions, so it is used to identify substances by comparison against known standards.
On a paper chromatogram, the solvent front travels 8.0 cm from the origin. A pigment spot travels 5.2 cm from the origin. Calculate its Rf value.

items: 1Identify the two distances, both measured from the same origin.Component = 5.2 cm; solvent front = 8.0 cm
2Divide the component's distance by the solvent front's distance.Rf = 5.2 / 8.0

blocks.x: Answer: Rf = 0.65
Column chromatography

In column chromatography, a continuous flow of solvent carries dissolved solutes (say, solutes A and B) down through a packed column. Because the solutes have differing affinities for the stationary phase, they migrate at different rates — for example, solute B, with a lower affinity for the stationary phase, would emerge (elute) from the column before solute A. The pH and temperature of the solvent can be varied to alter the separation and the timing of elution.

items: Spectrophotometry quantifies a coloured/absorbing substance by how much light of a chosen wavelength it absorbs.
Autoradiography visualises and localises where a radioactively labelled substance ends up, using photographic emulsion sensitive to radioactive emissions.
Chromatography separates a mixture into its individual components based on differential movement between a stationary and a mobile phase; the Rf value identifies each separated component.
